My aunt Renata blows glass in a converted garage at the end of a gravel road, and the summer I turned fourteen she decided I was old enough to make something. The furnace sat in the middle of the room like a squat brick animal, and when she opened its door the heat reached across the floor and pressed against my face. Inside, the melted glass glowed the color of the sun at the bottom of a sunset.

The first step, she said, was the gather. I was to dip the end of a long steel pipe into the furnace, turn it slowly, and draw out a glowing lump about the size of a plum. She made it look like stirring soup. When I tried, my hands shook so badly that the pipe knocked against the edge of the opening, and I pulled it out with nothing on the end at all.

"Again," she said.

On the third try I brought out a gather, lopsided and dripping, and Renata guided me to the steel table where I was supposed to roll it smooth. I kept thinking about how hot it was, how one careless turn could send it sliding off the pipe and onto the floor, or onto my shoe. My shirt was soaked through. Every few seconds I glanced at the clock above the workbench, as if it could tell me how much longer I had to hold on.

She showed me how to blow into the pipe, a short puff and then my thumb over the end, so that the trapped air would swell the glass from inside. Nothing happened the first time. The second time, the lump grew a small, wobbling bubble, and I was so startled that I nearly dropped the pipe.

By the end of the afternoon I had made a paperweight, or something that was meant to be one. It was cloudy and slightly flat on one side, with a single trapped bubble near the top. Renata set it in the annealing oven, where it would cool slowly overnight so that it would not crack.

The next morning it was waiting on the shelf, cool enough to hold. I turned it over in my palm and saw the bubble catch the light. I have made better pieces since then, but I still cannot stand near an open furnace without feeling my heart speed up, and I still count the seconds until the glass is safely on the table.

The furnace sat in the middle of the room like a squat brick animal, and when she opened its door the heat reached across the floor and pressed against my face. Inside, the melted glass glowed the color of the sun at the bottom of a sunset.

The first step, she said, was the gather. I was to dip the end of a long steel pipe into the furnace, turn it slowly, and draw out a glowing lump about the size of a plum. She made it look like stirring soup. When I tried, my hands shook so badly that the pipe knocked against the edge of the opening, and I pulled it out with nothing on the end at all.

"Again," she said.

On the third try I brought out a gather, lopsided and dripping, and Renata guided me to the steel table where I was supposed to roll it smooth. I kept thinking about how hot it was, how one careless turn could send it sliding off the pipe and onto the floor, or onto my shoe. My shirt was soaked through. Every few seconds I glanced at the clock above the workbench, as if it could tell me how much longer I had to hold on.

She showed me how to blow into the pipe, a short puff and then my thumb over the end, so that the trapped air would swell the glass from inside. Nothing happened the first time. The second time, the lump grew a small, wobbling bubble, and I was so startled that I nearly dropped the pipe.

By the end of the afternoon I had made a paperweight, or something that was meant to be one. It was cloudy and slightly flat on one side, with a single trapped bubble near the top. Renata set it in the annealing oven, where it would cool slowly overnight so that it would not crack.

The next morning it was waiting on the shelf, cool enough to hold. I turned it over in my palm and saw the bubble catch the light. I have made better pieces since then, but I still cannot stand near an open furnace without feeling my heart speed up, and I still count the seconds until the glass is safely on the table.

Every Saturday morning when I was ten, my grandfather and I took the number 9 bus to the end of the line, where the city gave way to warehouses and a strip of tidal marsh. He had worked for forty years as a welder at the shipyard there, and although the yard had closed long before I was born, he liked to walk along its fence and point out where everything had been.

"That's where the cranes stood," he would say, nodding at an empty lot full of thistles. "Four of them. You could see them from our kitchen." Then he would tell me about the ships: a tanker that took two years to build, a ferry with a dining room paneled in teak, a research vessel that had gone all the way to Antarctica. He remembered their names the way other people remember birthdays.

I listened less closely than I should have. I was ten, and the marsh was full of fiddler crabs, and I spent a good part of each walk crouched at the edge of the water, waiting for them to come out of their holes. My grandfather never seemed to mind. He would stand beside me with his hands in his jacket pockets and wait, and when a crab finally appeared he was as pleased as I was.

On the way home we always stopped at a diner near the bus stop, where he ordered black coffee and I ordered pancakes with too much syrup. He kept a pencil stub in his shirt pocket, and on the back of the paper placemat he would draw the outline of whatever ship he had been describing, the hull first and then the decks, until the placemat looked like a page from an engineering book.

I kept a few of those placemats. They are soft and stained now, folded into a shoebox in my closet, and the drawings on them are better than I remembered: steady lines, careful proportions, every railing and porthole in its place. Looking at them, I understand something I was too young to see then. He was not only telling me about the ships. He was showing me what it had meant to him to help make them.

Last year the city built a park on the old shipyard land. There is a plaque near the entrance that lists some of the ships built there. I took the bus out to read it, and I was glad to find the research vessel among them, the one that went to Antarctica, spelled exactly the way he used to say it.

item.passage:
In the past ten years, many cities have begun turning off their public drinking fountains. The reasons given are practical. Fountains break, they must be cleaned, and they cost money to inspect. Bottled water is everywhere, the argument goes, and most people carry a water bottle of their own.

Each of these points is true as far as it goes, and none of them goes very far. A drinking fountain is one of the few things in a city that anyone may use, at any time, without paying and without being a customer. A child coming home from a game, a delivery rider in July, an older person walking to the clinic, a visitor who forgot a bottle: all of them can drink. When the fountain disappears, the cost of a drink of water stays behind. It moves to the person who is thirsty.

The money saved is also smaller than it looks. In one mid-sized city whose budget I examined, maintaining all two hundred public fountains cost less each year than the city spent on decorative flower displays along a single downtown boulevard. Nobody suggested removing the flowers.

There is a quieter cost as well. A city that shuts off its fountains is telling its residents something about what it owes them. Public restrooms, benches and fountains are small things, but together they mark the difference between a city built for people who are spending money and a city built for everyone who lives in it.

Defenders of the closures point out that fountains can carry germs. Modern fountains, however, can be fitted with spouts for filling bottles, which never touch a mouth, and they can be cleaned on the same schedule as any other public surface. The problem is maintenance, and maintenance is a choice.

A few cities have gone the other way. They have repaired old fountains, added new ones in parks and transit stations, and printed maps showing where they are. Water use at the new stations has been high, especially in summer, and complaints about cost have been rare. The lesson seems plain enough. When a city makes water easy to find, people drink it, and a small public good does its quiet work.

In the summer of 1926, the town of Pellham, Kansas, finished building a steel water tower on the rise behind the grain elevator. It held sixty thousand gallons, it could be seen from eleven miles away, and it was, in the words of the town newspaper, "the tallest thing between here and Wichita." It was also, for the first two years of its life, unpainted.

The trouble began at the first town meeting after the tower went up. The mayor proposed painting it silver, which he said would look modern and reflect the summer heat. A councilman who owned the hardware store proposed green, a color he happened to have in stock. The high school principal wanted the school colors, maroon and gold, in stripes. A retired sea captain, the only one in the county, insisted that any tall structure ought to be painted in red and white bands so that it could be seen in fog. Pellham had never had a fog in its recorded history.

The debate went on for nineteen months. It filled the letters page of the Pellham Courier so completely that the editor began printing the letters in alphabetical order by the color they supported. A petition for silver collected two hundred signatures; a petition for green collected two hundred and four, several of them, it was later discovered, from the same household. At one meeting the principal brought a cardboard model of the tower painted in stripes, and the sea captain brought a foghorn.

In the meantime the tower began to rust. Orange streaks ran down its legs, and by the second spring a farmer driving into town remarked that it looked like a giant tin can left out in the rain. This, at last, produced agreement of a kind. At the meeting of March 1928 the council voted, eight to one, to paint the tower immediately in whatever color could be applied before the summer.

The color that could be applied before the summer turned out to be green, since the hardware store had forty gallons of it on hand. The tower was painted green in April. The councilman who owned the store was re-elected that fall by a comfortable margin.

The tower still stands. It has been repainted six times since 1928, always green, and the town's high school teams, though their colors remain maroon and gold, are known throughout the county as the Pellham Water Tower.

An octopus resting on a reef can vanish in less than a second. One moment it is a reddish lump against the rocks; the next it has taken on the speckled gray of the stone beneath it, raised small bumps on its skin to match the stone's texture, and flattened its body against the surface. A diver who looked away for a moment might never find it again.

The color change is controlled by thousands of tiny sacs in the octopus's skin, each filled with pigment and surrounded by a ring of muscle. When the muscle tightens, the sac stretches open and its color spreads across a wider patch of skin. When the muscle relaxes, the sac shrinks to a dot. Because each sac is wired directly to the nervous system, the octopus can change hundreds of them at once, faster than a person can blink.

What has long puzzled biologists is that most octopuses appear to be color-blind. Their eyes contain only one kind of light-detecting cell, which in animals such as humans would mean an inability to tell red from green. Yet an octopus placed on a red background will turn reddish, and one placed on a mottled green one will turn mottled green.

Several explanations have been proposed. One is that the octopus judges brightness and pattern rather than color, and that matching those is enough to fool most predators. Another, more surprising, is that the skin itself may sense light. Researchers have found light-sensitive proteins in octopus skin, the same kind found in eyes, which raises the possibility that an octopus can respond to its surroundings with its whole body as well as with its eyes. A third suggests that the unusual U-shaped pupil of many octopuses may let them extract some color information from the way different colors blur. None of these ideas has yet been confirmed, and more than one may turn out to be true.

Whatever the answer, the result is one of the most sophisticated disguises in the animal world. An octopus is soft-bodied, without shell or bone, and almost every larger animal in the sea would happily eat it. Its survival depends on staying unseen, and over millions of years it has become extraordinarily good at that. To watch one melt into a rock is to see a problem solved with an elegance that human engineers have yet to copy.

In the spring of 1894, a photographer named Edith Varney set up a large wooden camera on a tripod at the corner of Front and Mill Streets in the river town of Ashby and began taking pictures. She worked there, on and off, for the next thirty years. By the time she stopped, she had made more than four thousand glass-plate negatives of a single small town: its storefronts and floods, its parades and funerals, its children on the courthouse steps.

Varney had learned photography from her father, who ran a portrait studio, and she took over the business when he died. Portraits paid the bills. The street photographs, which she made on her own time and mostly at her own expense, did not. She printed a few for the newspaper and sold others as postcards, but most of the negatives went into wooden crates in the studio's back room, labeled in her tidy hand with a date and a street name.

Glass negatives of that period are remarkable objects. Because each plate is large, often eight by ten inches, a print made from it can show astonishing detail: the lettering on a shop sign half a block away, the buttons on a stranger's coat. Historians who have studied Varney's surviving plates have used them to date buildings, identify forgotten businesses and trace how the town changed after the railroad arrived.

Only about six hundred of her plates survive. After her death in 1931, the studio was sold, and the new owner had no use for the crates. Some were given away. Many were sold by the pound to a local nursery, whose owner scraped the images from the glass and used the clear panes to build a greenhouse. For decades, sunlight passed through what had once been pictures of Ashby, falling on rows of tomato seedlings.

The surviving plates were found in 1978 in the attic of a house two streets from the old studio, wrapped in newspaper and stacked in a cardboard box. No one knows how they got there. They are now kept at the state historical society, where they are among the most requested items in the collection.

It is impossible to look at them without thinking of the ones that are gone. Each surviving plate is a reminder of six others that were scraped clean, and of the streets, faces and afternoons that will now never be seen again.
